newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus leader presses on with controversial poll.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader presses on with controversial poll.

text.p: Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko, locked in a bitter row with parliament, held out an olive branch to deputies on Thursday but vowed to press on with a controversial referendum aimed at boosting his powers.

Lukashenko, whose planned referendum on a new constitution would grant him a 10-year mandate, also told the chamber that Russian President Boris Yeltsin had expressed support for the vote, due to take place on November 7.

Sounding a conciliatory note, Lukashenko suggested widening parliament's powers under the new constitution, provided that deputies shelve plans for a separate referendum on their own proposed constitution planned for November 24.
Their constitution entails abolishing the post of president.
If parliament accepted his suggestion, Lukashenko said: "We would have demonstrated a common will and shown the people we have the ability to compromise."

He said he was ready to give deputies the right to form an upper parliamentary chamber under his proposed constitution and to allow them to serve out their full five-year term until 2000. Future parliaments will be elected for just four years.
Lukashenko also said parliament would be able to impeach the president with two-thirds of the vote instead of three-quarters as he had previously proposed in his new constitution.
However he said he would not compromise over the date of his referendum, commemorated in Soviet times as the anniversary of the 1917 Bolshevik revolution.
"This date is already in the people's minds," he said, adding that he would not use force to resolve his dispute with parliament.
Deputies are due to debate Lukashenko's proposals on Friday but some were quick to denounce the proposed deal.
"This is not a compromise because none of the proposals touch on the main issue -- the concentration of all power in presidential hands," said liberal deputy Alexander Dobrovolsky.

Lukashenko, elected Belarus' first post-Soviet president in 1994, has since suspended trade unions, shut down newspapers and put the brakes on market reforms. Some 200 people were jailed for demonstrating against his community pact with Moscow.
In Moscow, the presidential press office said on Thursday that Yeltsin and Lukashenko, speaking by telephone, had agreed to meet next week.
"The attitude of the Russian leadership towards the referendum (on November 7) is positive. Boris Yeltsin has approved the idea of holding the referendum," Lukashenko said.
"After the vote I will boost our integration with Russia."

The two presidents signed a framework agreement last April on forming a loose union between Russia and Belarus. But Yeltsin has expressed concern over the conflict between Lukashenko and parliament and has urged him to seek a compromise solution.
Lukashenko has called an "All-Belarussian meeting" on October 19 to seek backing for his referendum, but opposition members say it will be attended only by loyal apparatchiks.

The head of the Central Electoral Commission Nikolai Gonchar said on Wednesday his body would not recognise either of the two planned referendums because his commission did not have time to draw up lists of voters.
